Eleven-year-old Marley Dias has gotten a lot of attention for being the girl who got sick of reading about white boys and their dogs and did something about it.
#1000BlackGirlBooks, the soon-to-be seventh grader’s campaign to get more books about girls who look like her into the hands of fellow readers, has been featured on shows including “Ellen” and “Today.” Plenty of magazines, including Ebony, which placed her on its
2016 list of “coolest black kids in America
,” have taken notice, too.
Now her campaign has expanded, and includes efforts to change reading lists in her own neighborhood, as well as a national literacy tour.
“I got a little tired of doing it when I missed one of my sixth-grade field trips,” she said. “But I love #1000BlackGirlBooks, and I’m going to keep doing it.”
Marley started the book drive as a sixth-grader, in November 2015.
“I wasn’t seeing black girls in the books I was assigned to read at my school, and I was tired of only reading about white boys and dogs,” she recalled from a conference room in a West Orange office building, where she was sorting books in preparation for the ongoing tour, which has so far has brought her to Washington, D.C., and Atlanta.
“Old Yeller,” “Shiloh” and “Where the Red Fern Grows” – all books about white boys and their dogs– were on the assigned lists at St. Cloud Elementary, where Marley had attended fifth grade. Favorites of hers, more recent titles like “Brown Girl Dreaming” by
Jacqueline Woodson
and “Esperanza Rising” by
Pam Munoz Ryan
, were not.
The imbalance bothered her, and she wanted to correct it, because books have served her well.
“A lot of books have lessons that are good lessons, like tie your shoelaces or be careful what you wish for,” said Marley, who aspires to be a magazine editor. “But if you don’t have a common trait with the character in the book, you don’t remember the lesson as well. If you do have a common trait, there’s always something connecting you back.”
She also thought it was important for people outside her demographic to get a sense of what it’s like to be a black girl, much the same way she had gotten an inkling of how it feels to be a white boy by reading books like “Old Yeller.”
“We have different stories, different points of view, different issues in the world,” she said. “Other people should be able see that.”
Janice Johnson Dias, Marley’s mother and a sociology professor at John Jay College of Criminal Justice in Manhattan, thought so, too. But she wasn’t going to drop everything to help her daughter gather books.
“Everyone thinks, because it’s a young person, ‘Oh, it must be the mom’s idea.’ But I was like, no, I have other stuff to do. This is her idea,” said Ms. Johnson Dias, who co-founded
GrassROOTS
, a social action group that promotes girls’ wellness, with Tariq “Black Thought” Trotter of the Roots.
So it was up to Marley. She decided to collect 1,000 books, and to donate those books to a school in rural St. Mary, Jamaica, where Ms. Johnson Dias grew up. She took to social media. The responses there didn’t all match her intentions.
“There was some hostility,” Ms. Johnson Dias said. “One person wrote on Facebook that if she wanted to see black people, she should read obituaries. And I now credit that person for the bigness of the campaign. Because people saw how awful it was, and they were asking, ‘Who is this troll?’”
Those people eventually included Ellen DeGeneres. In January, Ms. DeGeneres handed Marley a check for $10,000 to buy books.
Soon Marley had collected more than 1,000 books.
The collecting and distributing of books is now only part of the campaign. The literacy tour, which is expected to stop in a different city every month until at least 2017 so Marley can talk about books and promote the ones she likes to other young readers, is another part.
Still another involves inspiring change closer to home, in her own school district.
“It’s not about replacing these books kids have been reading a gazillion years now,” said Marley, including “Where the Red Fern Grows,” which she found especially vexing because it was on both her fifth and sixth grade reading lists. “It’s about including more diverse titles.”
She’s already had some luck:
Rita Williams-Garcia’s
2014 book, “One Crazy Summer,” about three black girls during the tumultuous summer of 1968, was added to St. Cloud Elementary School’s curriculum this spring.
Marley’s commitment to maintaining the campaign has made her a hero to one of her own heroes – Ms. Woodson, the author of “Brown Girl Dreaming.”
“She is my dream 21
st
-century person, in terms of realizing something needs to be changed and making it happen,” said Ms. Woodson.
